narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 55.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) of your class, far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among students who were accepted. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor, and it worked in the opposite direction. At 36, your score is only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, so it modestly pulled the prediction toward passing. However, this positive effect was not strong enough to overcome the negative impact of your academic ranking.

Your family income bracket (middle income) was the third most important feature. It gave a small additional push toward failure, though its influence was much weaker than the other two.

Taken together, the model concluded your overall profile indicated more than a 50% chance of failing the bar. To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic performance and class ranking in law school, as that factor carried the most weight in this decision. Consider targeted bar-prep resources early and, if possible, retake the LSAT to raise your score further. These steps can meaningfully shift future predictions in your favor.
